cards.explanation: The answer is allies. Bera king of Sodom, Birsha king of Gomorrah and the other three kings came to the Valley of Siddim as allies, which puts all five on one side. They're on the same team against the four kings. Five kings agreeing on one plan, and I can't get two ovens to agree on one temperature.

The answer is rebelled. For twelve years Sodom's side was subject to Chedorlaomer, and in the thirteenth year they rebelled. Then in the fourteenth year, Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him went out (Gen 14:5). That's quite a way to end twelve years of going along with it.

The answer is False. The five kings did not beat the four. The kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, and some of their men fell into the tar pits. The survivors ran to the hill country, and then the four kings seized all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah.

The answer is tar pits. The Valley of Siddim was full of them, and as the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, some men fell into the pits. The survivors fled to the hill country. I think this part of the story hurts, so I'll just say it plainly and leave it there.

The answer is Lot, Abram's nephew. The four kings carried him off along with his possessions, since Lot was living in Sodom. Once Abram heard that his relative had been captured, he mobilized his men (Gen 14:14). So this part of the story turns on family.

The answer is that he sets out after the four kings. Abram mobilized the 318 trained men born in his household, and they set out in pursuit as far as Dan. He heard his relative was captured and he moved. No committee meeting.

The answer is that he divides his forces at night. During the night, Abram divided his forces and routed Chedorlaomer's army. Then he pursued them as far as Hobah, north of Damascus. He had 318 trained men, and I get nervous just dividing a batch of dough in broad daylight.

The answer is True. Abram retrieved all the goods, as well as his relative Lot and his possessions, together with the women and the rest of the people. So the goods came back with the people. That's a big result for 318 men.

The answer is bread and wine. Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought them out to Abram, and the text says he was priest of God Most High. Abram had just come back from a long chase, so I'd say that's a table worth sitting at.
The answer is True. Melchizedek is king of Salem, and the text says he was priest of God Most High. Two jobs, one man. Meanwhile, I'm still working on keeping one hat straight.

The answer is delivering Abram's enemies into his hand. Melchizedek says, "…blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand." He's speaking of the rescue Abram had just done. Melchizedek puts the praise on God Most High.

The answer is Melchizedek, king of Salem. After he blessed Abram, Abram gave him a tenth of everything. This came after Abram returned from defeating Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him (Gen 14:17). A tenth of everything, and I get dramatic about the last cookie in the box.
The answer is goods. The king of Sodom says, "Give me the people, but take the goods for yourself." On paper, it's a generous offer. Hold onto it, because Abram has something to say about it.

The answer is False, friends! The king of Sodom offers Abram the goods, but Abram says no. He tells the king he has raised his hand to the LORD God Most High, and he won't accept even a thread or a strap of a sandal. He doesn't want the king saying, 'I have made Abram rich' (Gen 14:21-23). So he refuses the whole pile, down to a shoelace-sized scrap. I once got nervous turning down a cracked cookie, and this man turned down a king.

The answer is so the king can't say he made Abram rich. That's the reason Abram gives. He says he won't accept anything, "…lest you should say, ‘I have made Abram rich.’" He wants the king to have nothing to say about that. Not one thread.

The answer is True, friends! Abram tells the king he will accept nothing except what his men have eaten and the share for the men who went with him. Then he names Aner, Eshcol and Mamre, and says they may take their portion (Gen 14:24). He doesn't force their hand either way. He only says that the share is theirs to take, and the text doesn't say what they did.
